title: MGCs: The Power Is in the Middle
author: Stuart, Dave Jr.
summary: Veteran teacher Dave Stuart Jr. describes refining his 'Moments of Genuine Connection' (MGC) strategy during a district PD visit, clarifying that tracking these brief check-ins is not meant for students a teacher naturally connects with or already worries about, but for the overlooked 'middle' group, quiet, standoffish, or simply undemonstrative students. He illustrates with a real classroom example, a freshman named Adam, showing how one brief, genuine conversation shifted the relationship, and argues that consistently reaching this middle group builds a teacher's credibility across an entire class rather than just with popular or at-risk students. He closes by noting the strategy benefits the teacher as much as the student.
points: Clarifies that MGC tracking is specifically for the overlooked 'middle' third of students, not the ones a teacher already checks in with by default.
Illustrates with a concrete classroom exchange showing how a single genuine question shifted a shy student's engagement.
Argues consistent outreach to this middle group builds comprehensive teacher credibility, not just favor with popular or at-risk students.
Notes the strategy's psychological benefit accrues to the teacher, not only the student.
quotes: MGC tracking is NOT for the two groups of students you and I will tend to check-in with regularly just on default teacher mode.

MGC tracking is PRIMARILY for the middle group of students who don't fall into the two categories above: the quiet ones, the standoffish ones, the shy ones, the ones who are just there doing what they're meant to do but not drawing attention to themselves.
Adam, what got you interested in computer science? [Listen.] What do you like to do outside of school? [Listen.] Very cool. Well listen, Adam, I'm glad I get to be your teacher this year.

By simply attempting these moments with that middle group on a regular basis, a teacher will begin to develop a robust and comprehensive Credibility across the whole student body, not just the kids who tend to be popular or the at-risk ones.

The person who most benefits from the MGC strategy is, in my view, the teacher. There is something about attempting to connect with 150+ diverse human beings each year that inevitably deepens and widens my soul.
